practicalQuestion: Across a seven-day period containing competition, travel, limited field time, and mixed athlete availability, how should sports performance staff allocate strength, speed, conditioning, and recovery exposures while defining individual progress, hold, or adjust criteria?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate roster with starters, non-starters, and athletes in modified participation
decisionContext.sport: Team sport with shared field and weight-room resources
decisionContext.outcome: Build a coherent plan that preserves competition readiness and appropriate chronic exposure
decisionContext.constraints: Travel; one full-team field session; varied recent minutes; no universal readiness marker; medical plans remain controlling for restricted athletes

evidenceConfidence.rationale: The pack has relevant evidence on where high-speed and near-maximal speed exposures fall in a match week, and on workload gaps for players with fewer match minutes. It comes mostly from single professional soccer teams, one multi-team observational study, a coach survey and expert commentary. Sources disagree on whether the day two before a match should hold near-maximal speed work or be a taper day. Strength placement is described only by one team's session content and a coach survey of hamstring exercises, with no outcome testing. There is nothing on collegiate in-season rosters and no validated individual progress, hold or adjust criteria. Options are presented without choosing one.

dimensions.sourceReview: Every claim is checked against original source text. Designs include one retrospective multi-team observational study, single-team descriptive and cohort studies, a coach survey, a systematic review, an expert commentary and a collegiate case series. Several statements in the survey, review and commentary are cited from earlier work and are labelled that way.
dimensions.directness: Direct for the timing of high-speed and near-maximal speed running and for starter versus non-starter load gaps. Descriptive only for strength placement within the week. Absent for travel-day training changes and validated individual decision criteria.
dimensions.consistency: Consistent that high-speed loading is concentrated mid-week and that low-minute players accumulate less weekly load. Inconsistent on near-maximal speed exposure two days before a match. One peak-demand study lists the day after the match among the highest training peaks in its abstract but states in its conclusion that sessions four and three days out usually exceeded it.
dimensions.transferability: Nearly all data come from professional or reserve-squad soccer, mostly single clubs. The only collegiate source is a case series from one American football team, with injuries in weight-room sessions mostly outside the season. Transfer to a collegiate team sport with shared resources is untested.

bottomLine.text: Professional soccer studies describe high-speed and peak-demand exposures concentrated mid-week, away from both matches, and their authors recommend topping up players with limited match minutes. Whether near-maximal speed work belongs two days before competition is contested: one observational study links it to fewer match hamstring injuries, while most surveyed coaches do sprint work three days out. The evidence does not supply validated individual progress, hold or adjust rules, so those must be locally defined.

actions.title: Recently played athletes: keep the first two post-match days low in hamstring-demanding work
actions.text: Surveyed coaches of European professional soccer teams, answering for players heavily involved in the last match, generally avoid high hamstring neuromuscular demands on the two days after a match. In one professional team, high-speed running sat on the central days of the week, and its authors recommend that placement. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): with travel and one full-team field session, place that session on a central day where possible.

actions.title: Strength exposures: consider descriptive placement patterns
actions.text: In a coach survey, most teams used hip- or knee-dominant hamstring exercises four days before the match, and general strength tasks were typically done before training or in the warm-up. In one professional team's seven-day week, strength training made up about a quarter of the session three days before the match and preventive strength about 15 percent two days before. These describe practice, not tested outcomes. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): place the heavier weight-room exposure on a central day and keep strength work lighter close to competition.

actions.title: Near-maximal speed timing: choose and document one of two options
actions.text: Option A: schedule individual exposure above 95 percent of maximal speed two days before competition. In elite football data, no match hamstring injuries occurred when such exposures fell on that day (480 player-turnarounds), but the design was observational and, pooled across turnarounds, injury rates did not differ with versus without near-maximal exposure. The authors add that the days four and three before the match should then be adjusted so players do not arrive fatigued, and that for six- to eight-day turnarounds this may concern the whole squad. Option B: concentrate high-speed and sprint work mid-week and taper the day two before competition. One professional team made that its lowest day, most surveyed coaches do sprint work three days out, and some methodologies prefer tapering two days out. The evidence does not settle which is better.

actions.title: Low-minute and non-playing athletes: plan compensatory exposure
actions.text: Players with more match minutes accumulated more weekly load; weekly high-speed and sprint running was double for full-match players compared with non-playing players. Authors recommend increasing training workloads for non-starters. One team's compensatory small-sided session the day after the match did not seem to give enough high-speed and sprint overload, and the authors cite earlier work suggesting running circuits with supra-maximal running could. One study suggests the day before, the day of, and the day after a match as possible compensation sessions. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): with only one full-team field session, compensation may need small-group time outside it.

actions.title: Modified participation athletes: follow the medical plan and watch substituted loading
actions.text: In one collegiate football team, six of seven pectoralis major injuries occurred in athletes with a preexisting lower body injury whose work was restricted to the upper body, including upper body cardio workouts, and players were attempting personal record bench presses every two weeks. The authors believe concurrent upper body strength and endurance work was the key factor, and they cite a recommendation to limit one-repetition maximum bench press attempts to two or three per year. This is author belief from an off-season case series. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): when lower body work is restricted, review how much upper body strength, maximal testing and conditioning is stacked in the same week.

actions.title: Define local progress, hold or adjust criteria
actions.text: Expert commentary recommends combining objective load measures with perceived exertion and wellness, reporting a few key metrics, and, in recovery planning, considering how players who start sequential matches differ from those who stay on the bench. One study notes a cited suggestion that training monotony above 2 arbitrary units raises injury risk, but its authors say reference values for their load metrics still need to be established. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): write explicit team rules for each group in advance, since no source validates a specific threshold.

monitoring.label: Individual near-maximal speed exposure
monitoring.text: Track whether and on which day each athlete reaches high percentages of their own maximal speed. In elite football, only 18 percent of three-day turnarounds and 72 percent of seven-day turnarounds included runs above 85 percent of maximal speed, using individual thresholds. Survey authors, citing that same study among others, suggest reaching above 85 percent of maximum speed in one of the week's sessions; this is not independent support.

monitoring.label: Weekly accumulated load by match minutes
monitoring.text: Compare weekly high-speed and sprint exposure across athletes grouped by minutes played. More match time was associated with higher accumulated load, non-playing players reached about one match worth of weekly high-speed and sprint running, and non-starters may lack high-intensity demands if they follow the starters' regimen.

monitoring.label: Mixed objective and subjective check-ins, including after travel
monitoring.text: Pair objective load data with perceived exertion and wellness, using a few key metrics. A review cites a player survey in which two-thirds suggested travel may limit recovery, and a commentary notes there is no research-based evidence on managing travel fatigue, so note travel days in the record.

guardrails.text: The decision context states that medical plans remain controlling for athletes in modified participation. Expert commentary recommends improving communication among players, coaches and medical staff, citing earlier work showing little player and coach agreement on return-to-play decisions.

The near-maximal speed finding is an observational association. The authors state the design precludes causal conclusions, and pooled across turnarounds there was no difference in injury rate with versus without near-maximal exposure, so it should not be treated as a proven injury prevention rule.
Weekly distribution data and coach surveys describe what teams do, not what works best. Authors caution that results depend on each staff's training philosophy and that there is no strong consensus.

limitations.text: Most sources studied professional or reserve-squad soccer, often a single club. None studied a collegiate team sport roster with shared field and weight-room resources in season, and the only collegiate source is a case series in American football.
Single-team studies limit generalization. One load study analysed only six-day between-match weeks, and another states it is not large enough for full generalizations.

Match peak demands exceeded training at all intensities in one team, and another team's authors note they lacked data on whether sprint demands were enough to optimize fitness, so the pack does not show how much training exposure is enough to preserve chronic load.

whatCouldChange.text: Prospective or controlled studies comparing near-maximal speed on the day two before competition with mid-week placement could resolve the main tension.
Collegiate studies that link compensatory exposure for low-minute athletes to fitness, availability or injury outcomes could support a recommended direction.

evidenceTension.text: Elite football data found no match hamstring injuries when exposures above 95 percent of maximal speed occurred two days before a match, while injuries still occurred with no exposure or exposure three or more days out; pooled across turnarounds, though, injury rates did not differ with versus without near-maximal exposure. In contrast, one professional team made the day two before a match its lowest high-speed day, which its authors attribute to their own planning approach, most surveyed coaches report doing sprint training three days out rather than two, and cited methodologies differ on whether that day prioritizes sprinting or tapering.

claims.text: In a retrospective observational study of elite football teams from top leagues, there were no match hamstring injuries when training exposures above 95 percent of maximal sprinting speed occurred two days before the match, while injuries still happened with no exposure or exposure three or more days before. The authors state the observational design precludes causal conclusions and that this timing may help mitigate match hamstring injuries.

evidence.excerpt: there were no match hamstring injuries when > 95% MSS exposures occurred at D-2, while in contrast, injuries still happened when players were not exposed at all, or when these exposures occurred at D-3 and/or earlier within the turnaround.

While the present observational study design precludes the examination of causal relationships, the programming of > 95% MSS exposures at D-2 may help mitigate match hamstring injury occurrences in elite football.

claims.text: In the same elite football data, longer turnarounds and lower speed thresholds produced more near-maximal speed exposures, for example 18, 45 and 72 percent of 3, 5 and 7 day turnarounds included runs above 85 percent of maximal speed. Exposures were marked using individual speed thresholds relative to each player's maximal speed.

evidence.excerpt: The longer the length of the turnarounds and the lower the speed thresholds, the greater the number (and proportion) of near-to-MSS exposures (e.g., 18%, 45% and 72% of turnarounds with > 85% runs for 3, 5 and 7-turnarounds, respectively).
occurred using individual speed thresholds at > 85%, > 90%

claims.text: In one professional football team, regardless of microcycle length, the central days (five, four and three days before the match) accumulated more high-speed, very high-speed and sprint running than post-match and pre-match days, and the day two before the match required the least stimulus. The authors attribute this to the team's own planning approach, which differs from others such as tactical periodization where that day is not the lowest.
